title: My soul doth magnify (Luke 1:46–55)
hook: Mary's song turns the world over: the proud scattered, the hungry filled

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Visitation: two pregnant women in a doorway, a baby who leaped, and the line go to the one who understands. Today, what Mary says next.

Mary stands in Elizabeth's doorway, just blessed as the mother of her Lord. What would you expect a young girl in her position to say? Thank you. Maybe something shy. Instead, Luke says, she opens her mouth and sings. Not a lullaby. A song about the world being turned upside down. Kings pulled off their thrones. Hungry people fed. Rich people sent home with nothing. Read slowly, it's a fierce song.
screen: `JUST BLESSED IN A DOORWAY.` → `SHE SINGS.` → `A SONG ABOUT THE WORLD UPSIDE DOWN.`

segments.voice: It opens, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "My soul doth magnify the Lord. And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." In Latin, the first word is Magnificat, magnifies, and that's what the song has been called for many centuries. To magnify is to make bigger, like a magnifying glass. Mary isn't making God bigger than he is. She's making him big enough to see. Then she says why: because he has looked on the lowliness of his handmaid. A young woman from a town in Galilee called Nazareth. Then the song turns outward, and turns the world over. "He hath put down the mighty from their seat, and hath exalted the humble. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away." Notice the tense. Hath put down. Hath filled. She sings as though it's already happened. The song is full of older songs. It echoes, line by line, the prayer of Hannah in the book of Samuel, another woman who was given a child against the odds, and who also sang about the poor being raised from the dust. Mary sings in the words of her people's scriptures. The Church sings or says the Magnificat every evening. It's the high point of Evening Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours, the psalms from day twenty-one. Monks, nuns and priests all over the world stand for it. And every evening, the same promise goes out again: the lowly are lifted.
screen: `MAGNIFICAT — MAKE HIM BIG ENOUGH TO SEE.` · `THE LOWLINESS OF HIS HANDMAID.` · `THE MIGHTY DOWN, THE HUMBLE UP.` · `HANNAH'S SONG, SUNG AGAIN.` · then, large: `THE LOWLY ARE LIFTED.`

segments.voice: If you can, find Luke chapter one, verses forty-six to fifty-five, and read the Magnificat aloud once, slowly, as if it were your own song; if you can't look it up, just say its first line: my soul doth magnify the Lord. Then sit with it: what in your life feels small today, and what would it look like to be lifted? If you pray, you can make the song your prayer.
Magnificat. Mary's song, the Latin for magnifies: the proud scattered, the hungry filled, and the lowly lifted.
Your line: the lowly are lifted. It's Mary's song, and Hannah's before her. Day twenty-three, done.

howItsDone: The Magnificat is sung or said every evening at Vespers, Evening Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours, usually standing and making the sign of the cross as it begins.

original.note: Latin: my soul magnifies the Lord. the first words gave the song its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty hymn about Mary.
what it means: Mary's own song, turning the world over: the proud scattered, the hungry filled, the lowly lifted.
what a scholar hears: a mosaic of Old Testament songs, above all Hannah's (1 Samuel 2:1–10, 1 Kings 2 in the Douay-Rheims); sung daily at Vespers for many centuries.
